instructions: At least 3 hours ahead, or the night before: rinse the rice well under cold water. In a separate bowl, rinse the chana dal, toor dal, moong dal and urad dal together until the water runs mostly clear.
Put the rice and the dried red chilies in one bowl and cover with cold water. Cover the dals with cold water in another bowl. Leave both to soak for 3 to 4 hours.

Drain the rice and the chilies. Add them to a blender with a 1/2 inch piece of the ginger, the cumin seeds and 1/4 cup water. Blend to a thick, slightly coarse batter, then transfer it to a large bowl.
Drain the dals and add them to the blender with 1/4 cup water. Blend until thick and slightly coarse. Transfer to the bowl with the rice batter.
Finely chop 3 tbsp of the onion and 2 tbsp of the cilantro. Stir them into the batter along with the asafoetida and the salt.
Check the batter. It should be thick like pancake batter. Stir in a splash of water if it's too thick to spread.
Heat a large nonstick or cast iron skillet over medium heat. Wipe it with a little of the oil on a paper towel.
Pour a scant 1/3 cup of batter into the center and spread it quickly into a circle about 6 inches wide. Drizzle 1/2 tsp oil around the edge.
Cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until the edges lift and the underside is golden.
Flip it and cook the other side for 2 minutes, until crisp in spots. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the rest of the batter. You should get about 8 adai.
Serve hot with the coconut chutney.
advance_prep_notes: Soak the rice and dals 3 to 4 hours ahead, or overnight
method_notes: Swasthi's (the lead) soaks rice and four dals, grinds them coarse and skips fermenting, so the batter can be cooked the same day. The dals and rice are about 1:1, as other adai recipes describe it. Dried red chilies cut to 2 and the ghee swapped for oil to keep it mild and vegan. Hing often contains wheat flour, so the list asks for a gluten-free one. The soaking is the make-ahead part; the batter itself is ready to cook right after grinding.
